strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and practically important gap: standard static metrics (mAP, F1) do not capture distance-dependent and temporally fluctuating detection reliability, which matters for safety-critical ADS/ADAS downstream control. The motivating Figure 1 example is convincing.

The SensorRainFall dataset, collected on the Virginia Smart Road under controlled clear vs. 64 mm/h simulated rain conditions with precise ground-truth distances, is a unique asset. Controlled weather variation while holding other factors constant is rare among public driving datasets and supports causal claims about weather effects.

The methodology is statistically principled rather than heuristic: penalized B-spline mean fitting, variance change-point detection via an SIC-based sequential hypothesis test (building on [15]), and a probabilistic PCD definition are clearly formalized, and the mPCD aggregation over threshold combinations is a sensible analogue of AUC.

Evaluation covers five strong, diverse detectors (Deformable DETR, Grounding DINO, DyHead, YOLOX, GLIP) under zero-shot conditions, and results (Table 2, 3) are internally consistent with the narrative: more change points and lower mPCD under rain; mPCD reveals model differences (e.g., Grounding DINO vs. DyHead) that mAP does not.
The authors promise public release of both dataset and evaluation code, which supports reproducibility of the proposed metric.
weaknesses: The dataset is very narrow as a benchmark: a single target object (one red sedan), ~595 frames total, one ego-vehicle trajectory, only two conditions, camera-only evaluation. Although camera, radar, and LiDAR data are claimed to be collected, only camera results are reported, so the multi-modal claim is unsupported. The general usefulness of the 'benchmark' is consequently limited.

Statistical assumptions are questionable. Confidence scores are not calibrated probabilities, so interpreting P(y_i > y_t) with a Gaussian model of the raw IoU×confidence score lacks semantic grounding. Moreover, consecutive frames along a single approach trajectory are strongly temporally correlated, violating the independence assumption on ε_i in Eq. (2), which likely inflates significance of change-point detection and understates uncertainty in PCD/mPCD. No confidence intervals or repeated-trial validation of PCD estimates are provided.

The evaluation of the metric's added value is thin. The claim that mPCD 'reveals differences not captured by mAP' rests on a single anecdote (DyHead vs. Grounding DINO). There is no controlled comparison against temporal extensions the authors themselves cite (e.g., stability-enhanced mAP [6], Average Delay [7]), so the positioning of PCD against related metrics is not empirically substantiated.

Some reported numbers raise concerns: AP_S/AP_M/AP_L are identical (0.982/0.956) across all five models in clear daylight, indicating degenerate size-based metrics on a single-object dataset; such metrics should have been omitted or discussed. Table 2 also shows YOLOX as the only model with more change points in clear weather, which is not analyzed.

Hyperparameters appear under-validated: K=10, order-3 splines, λ=0.6 fixed ('suffices in our case'), α=0.05; no sensitivity analysis of PCD to these choices is given, despite the sequential multi-change-point procedure being prone to over-segmentation.

Presentation errors undermine polish: the dataset and code URLs in the abstract are blank; Eq. (6) evaluates f(x_τ) inside residual sums where f(x_i) is intended; Section 5.1 says 'the model was trained' although all models are used zero-shot (inference only); Section 3 title/figure text inconsistently use 'SensorRainfall' vs. 'SensorRainFall'.

Eq. (10) defines PCD as max{x_i | P(y_i > y_t) > p_t}, but the underlying spline/segment model makes this quantity a function of arbitrary segment boundaries and extrapolated σ_i near the far end of the range, where data are sparse and scores collapse to zero; robustness of the PCD estimate in this regime is not demonstrated.

strengths: The SensorRainFall dataset addresses a genuine gap: perception evaluation under controlled weather conditions (controlled 64 mm/h rainfall on the Virginia Smart Road) with precise ground-truth distances, which naturalistic datasets like BDD100K or nuScenes cannot provide.

The core observation that detection confidence becomes unstable and heteroscedastic with distance (Figure 1, Figure 4) is real, well-motivated, and relevant to ADS/ADAS safety where downstream control relies on thresholded detections.

The statistical machinery (penalized spline mean estimation plus sequential SIC-based variance change-point testing) is carefully described and grounded in the literature, and the PCD/mPCD formulation (Eq. 10) is a reasonable probabilistic generalization of 'maximum reliable detection range'.

Experiments cover five representative SOTA detectors (both deterministic and open-vocabulary) under two weather conditions, with a threshold-sensitivity analysis (Figure 6) and comparison against standard metrics (mAP, AP50/75, APS/M/L), demonstrating cases (DyHead vs. Grounding DINO) where mPCD differentiates models that mAP does not.
weaknesses: Extremely narrow evaluation scope: the dataset contains a single target object (one red sedan) in a single class, ~600 images total (278 clear + 317 rainy), collected as sequential front-view frames of one drive scenario. Claims about 'perception characteristics of a system' and general ADS reliability are not supported by such limited data; there is no evidence PCD generalizes to other objects, scenes, lighting conditions, or datasets (acknowledged only briefly in the conclusion).

Methodological assumptions are questionable and insufficiently justified: (a) the IoU×confidence score is modeled as Gaussian within segments even though detection confidence is bounded [0,1], heavily skewed, and saturated at exactly 0 or 1 at long range (visible as flat lines of zeros in Figures 4-5); (b) Eq. 2 assumes independent errors, but consecutive frames of the same ego-approach sequence are strongly autocorrelated, invalidating the effective sample size and the change-point test's calibration; (c) uncertainty in the spline mean estimate f(x_i) is not propagated, and sigma_i is held constant across an entire segment despite the mean varying within it.

Several technical inconsistencies: Eq. 6 evaluates the residual likelihood at f(x_tau) rather than f(x_i) for all i; Table 2's arrow convention (performance 'improved or declined') is confusing since more change points indicates worse stability, yet upward arrows are attached to increased counts; the caption narrative in Section 5.2.1 cites the range [87.833, 190.611] for Grounding DINO clear daylight, mixing values that the table assigns to rainy conditions.

The dataset is advertised as multimodal (camera, radar, LiDAR), but all reported experiments use camera images only; the radar and LiDAR annotations are never evaluated or even shown, so a central selling point of the dataset remains unvalidated in the paper.

The claimed advantage over static metrics is thin: Table 3 shows mPCD rankings largely mirror mAP rankings; the single differentiating example (DyHead vs. Grounding DINO) is anecdotal, and no quantitative or statistical validation is provided that mPCD correlates better with downstream driving-safety outcomes.

Reproducibility and presentation problems: the abstract's dataset and code URLs are literally blank ('publicly available at , and the evaluation code is open-sourced at'), so the two central artifact claims are unverifiable; there are grammatical errors ('The section begins implementation details'), and the conclusion's closing remark about autonomy disrupting employment is out of place in a scientific paper.

The claim that SensorRainFall is 'the only publicly available dataset collected in a highly controlled environment' for perception evaluation is asserted without comparative survey; fog/rain/snow controlled datasets and ADAS sensor benchmarking efforts exist, and this overstatement weakens credibility.

Fixed hyperparameters (K=10 spline basis, lambda=0.6, alpha=0.05) are used with only a passing mention of cross-validation; no sensitivity analysis of the change-point detection to these choices is provided, despite the fact that PCD values depend directly on the detected change points.

strengths: The problem addressed is real and underexplored: standard static metrics (mAP, IoU, F1) do not capture distance-dependent, temporally fluctuating detection reliability, which matters for ADS/ADAS threshold-based control logic.

The SensorRainFall dataset, collected on the Virginia Smart Road with controlled rainfall (64 mm/h) vs. clear conditions and precise ground-truth distances, is a genuinely useful and scarce resource; the controlled setup (weather as the only varying factor) is more rigorous than naturalistic datasets.

The statistical machinery (penalized B-spline regression for the mean, SIC-based sequential variance change-point testing) is more principled than ad hoc thresholding, and is clearly described with appropriate references.

The mPCD aggregation over (pt, yt) thresholds, analogous to AUC, is a sensible way to summarize the metric across operating points, and the threshold trade-off analysis (Section 5.2.3) is informative.

Evaluation code is open-sourced and five representative detectors (including open-vocabulary models) are benchmarked under both conditions, with qualitative findings (rain reduces reliable range) consistent with expectations.
weaknesses: Statistical modeling assumptions are internally inconsistent and questionable. Within each segment, the mean is allowed to vary smoothly (via the spline) while the variance is treated as a single constant std over the whole segment; the reported sigma_i therefore conflates residual variance with mean curvature, potentially distorting P(y_i > y_t). Additionally, a Gaussian model is imposed on IoU x confidence, a variable bounded in [0,1] and heavily zero-inflated at long range (Figures 4-5 show scores pinned at zero), so tail probabilities used to define PCD are unreliable exactly where they matter.

The independence assumption (epsilon_i i.i.d.) ignores strong temporal/spatial autocorrelation in consecutive frames, which invalidates the change-point test's nominal significance level; no diagnostic or remedy is offered.

Scale and diversity of the empirical evidence are very limited: ~595 images, a single target object (one red sedan), a single scene, and only two weather conditions. Claims about 'safer and more robust ADS operation' and general utility of PCD are not supported at this scale, and the paper itself concedes evaluation is confined to detection on SensorRainFall.

The added value of mPCD over existing metrics is evidenced only anecdotally (one comparison: DyHead vs. Grounding DINO with similar mAP but different mPCD). No systematic analysis (e.g., rank correlations, case studies, or downstream control simulation) demonstrates that PCD captures information mAP/AP metrics miss.

The interpretation 'more variance change points = less stability' is asserted rather than validated; change-point counts on ~300 points with sequential testing are sensitive to hyperparameters (K=10, lambda=0.6 'pre-selected'), and no sensitivity analysis is provided.

Several clarity/correctness lapses undermine confidence: the dataset URL in the abstract is missing entirely; Section 5.1 says the 'model was trained' although models are used without fine-tuning; the discussion of Figure 4 mixes clear-daylight change-point values (29.407) with rainy-daylight segment ranges ([87.833, 190.611], 217.114), making the analysis hard to follow.

Figure 3 shows two change points labeled in a way that is hard to reconcile with the stated two-step procedure, and the discrepancy between PCD being a max over a discrete set of sampled distances vs. a continuous range is not addressed (interpolation uncertainty between sampled x_i is ignored).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and practically important gap: standard frame-level metrics (AP, AR, F1) do not capture distance-dependent reliability or the stochastic, heteroscedastic behavior of perception outputs, which matters for downstream ADS control. Figure 1 and the GLIP vs. DyHead example (Table 1, Example 2; Figure 5) convincingly show cases where conventional metrics and aPCD rank models differently in physically meaningful ways.

The statistical formulation is more principled than typical heuristic evaluation metrics: the mean is modeled with penalized B-spline regression, variance change points are detected via a likelihood-ratio/SIC-based sequential hypothesis test (Eqs. 6–9), and PCD is defined probabilistically. Section 5.3 provides simulation studies quantifying the sensitivity of change-point detection to sample size and effect size, which supports the reliability of the estimation procedure.

The SensorRainFall dataset is a real asset: collection in a controlled weather facility (with verified rainfall rates via laser disdrometry, DGPS target positions, ROS time-synchronization) with object-level and pixel-level annotations under four environmental conditions is rare, and the supplementary provides a thorough dataset description and complete per-model configurations.

The evaluation breadth is substantial: 10 modern detection/segmentation models (including open-vocabulary ones) across 16 experiment combinations, with full results for all variance change points and metrics provided in the supplementary (Tables 3–10).

The safety-envelope and flexible-threshold discussion (Section 5.2, Figure 7) gives a concrete operational interpretation of PCD and shows how threshold sensitivity varies with environmental conditions.
weaknesses: The key claim that PCD 'supports safer and more robust ADS operation' is not empirically validated. No experiment links PCD/aPCD to any downstream outcome (e.g., time-to-collision error, FCW/AEB performance, decision stability). The metric's added value over AP is shown only via qualitative case studies (Examples 2 and 3, which are cherry-picked from 16 experiments; the authors note the dominant pattern in 11/16 is actually agreement with traditional metrics). A correlation or decision-theoretic analysis would substantially strengthen the contribution.

The dataset is small and narrow in scope: 1,231 sequential images, two target objects (one sedan, one dummy pedestrian), a single track, and one fixed rainfall rate in the main text (64 mm/h) that contradicts the supplementary (20 and 40 mm/h). With only two object categories, the generality of PCD and of the benchmark rankings is unclear. The claim that it is 'the only publicly available dataset collected in a highly controlled environment' is asserted without comparative discussion of existing adverse-weather datasets.

Several methodological assumptions are under-justified: (1) the Gaussian distribution of IoU×confidence within segments is assumed but not tested, and IoU×confidence is bounded in [0,1] and heavily zero-inflated at long range (Figures 4–6), making normality and the resulting probability P_Y(y > y_thres) questionable; (2) sequential frames of the same ego-target pair violate the independence assumption in the likelihood; (3) the product of IoU and confidence is a heuristic combination whose behavior (e.g., a high-confidence detection with slightly loose IoU) is not analyzed; (4) the fixed penalty λ=0.6 and K=10 B-splines are stated to 'suffice' without sensitivity analysis, although spline smoothness directly affects change-point detection.

Internal inconsistencies and presentation problems undermine polish: missing dataset URL/code links in the abstract, an unnamed data-collection facility ('collected on the , a facility...') repeated in both main text and supplementary, the rainfall-rate contradiction noted above, leftover artifacts ('Mask R-CNN ok' in Table 9), and an incomplete final sentence in the conclusion ('while the broader societal impacts of full autonomy.').

The evaluation is zero-shot only (no fine-tuning on SensorRainFall), which is defensible for benchmarking pretrained models but means the dataset's utility for training/robustness research is untested. Additionally, in several conditions (e.g., rainy-night pedestrian segmentation, Table 10) all models fail almost completely (aPCD = 0), where PCD provides little discriminative information.

The aPCD 'volume under the PCD surface' is described only loosely (grid ranges for p_thres and y_thres are not fully specified), and the uncertainty of the PCD estimate itself (e.g., confidence intervals from the spline fit) is not propagated, despite the metric being framed as uncertainty-aware.

strengths: The core idea is sensible and practically motivated: measuring the maximum distance at which a perception system can reliably detect an object, accounting for the stochasticity of detection confidence, is a physically meaningful and operationally relevant complement to frame-level metrics like AP.

The methodological pipeline is more rigorous than typical heuristic metrics: penalized-spline mean estimation, formal variance change-point testing with SIC-based statistics, and a probabilistic definition of the reliability cutoff are all clearly grounded in established statistics, and two simulation studies (sample size and effect size) validate the change-point detection component.

The SensorRainFall dataset is a genuine asset: controlled weather/illumination conditions on a closed test track, multiple sensor modalities, GPS-recorded distances, and manual bounding-box and instance-mask annotations across four environmental conditions and two target objects.

The benchmark study is broad (10 detection/segmentation models, 16 condition-object-task combinations) and the paper demonstrates concretely, via Examples 2 and 3, cases where aPCD reveals distance-dependent reliability differences (e.g., GLIP's stable outputs vs. DyHead's high-variance 'failure tail') that aggregate metrics miss.

The threshold-parameterized PCD surface and 'safety envelope' concept (Figure 7) is a useful framing for deployment-oriented evaluation, since it lets practitioners tune strictness to the operational use case.
weaknesses: The manuscript appears unfinished and is below the presentation bar for publication. The abstract and Section 3 contain blank/incomplete references (e.g., 'https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/' with no identifier, 'evaluation code is available at https://github.com/' truncated, and the data collection facility is left as an unnamed blank in multiple places), a duplicated sentence in Section 3 ('The dataset includes both object-level and pixel-level annotations...' appears twice in near-identical form), a stray 'ok' in Table 9 ('Mask R-CNN ok'), and the truncated final sentence of the conclusion ('while the broader societal impacts of full autonomy.'). These are not mere style issues; the missing dataset/code links directly undermine the reproducibility claims.

There are material internal inconsistencies about the dataset. The main paper states all rainy conditions used 'a controlled rainfall rate of 64 mm/h [5]', while the supplementary material states two nominal rainfall intensities of 20 mm/h and 40 mm/h. The dataset is described as both '1,231 sequential front-view images' and collected at 'vehicle speed ranging between 10-55 mph', yet distances are reported as static per-image targets; the relationship between temporal sequencing, vehicle motion, and the distance-based analysis is never clarified, which matters greatly because sequential frames violate the independence assumptions underlying the change-point likelihood test (Eq. 7-9).

The dataset's evaluation value is limited: only two target objects (one sedan, one dummy pedestrian), a single track, and roughly 300 images per condition. Claiming it is 'the only publicly available dataset collected in a highly controlled environment' is unsupported and overstated given related rainy-weather driving datasets (e.g., ACDC, WeatherNet-style collections) that are not discussed. With two objects and strong spatial autocorrelation in sequential frames, the paper cannot substantiate general conclusions about model reliability.

The headline claim that aPCD 'captures meaningful differences... which traditional metrics fail to reflect' is under-evidenced and possibly cherry-picked. The authors themselves state that in 11 of 16 experiments aPCD aligns with traditional metrics; only three divergent examples are showcased. No quantitative comparison (e.g., correlation between aPCD and AP across all 16 experiments, or statistical significance of the divergences) is provided to establish when and why aPCD adds value.

Several methodological choices are under-justified or potentially problematic: (1) the IoU x confidence product is a heuristic; multiplying two bounded scores does not obviously yield the claimed 'joint measure' and the alternative of treating IoU and confidence separately is never compared; (2) assuming y_i ~ N(mu_i, sigma_i^2) for a bounded score in [0,1] with heavy zero-inflation at long range (visible in Figures 4-6) is a questionable normality assumption; (3) sigma_i is estimated as a constant per segment, yet heteroscedasticity is the paper's central motivation, so PCD can depend heavily on arbitrary change-point segmentation (Table 3 shows up to 5 detected change points, and 0 for several cases with no discussion of how PCD is computed then); (4) the fixed penalty lambda=0.6 and K=10 splines are asserted to 'suffice' without sensitivity analysis; (5) aPCD as a 'volume under the PCD surface' depends on the discretization of two thresholds and the sensitivity of aPCD to this grid is unexamined.

The evaluation protocol confounds model quality with domain gap. All models are applied zero-shot from COCO/Objects365 training to an unusual domain (dummy pedestrian in a poncho with a reported 'halo' effect, off-lane target positioning). The very low absolute scores (many AP values near 0, e.g., Table 10 rainy night all zeros) mean PCD is largely measuring fine-tuning-free domain transfer failure rather than distance-dependent reliability, and no fine-tuned baseline is provided to disentangle these effects.

Statistical rigor in the main experiments is weaker than in the simulations: no confidence intervals or uncertainty quantification on aPCD values are reported despite PCD being explicitly an uncertainty-aware metric; the sequential-dependence and multiple-testing issues in the sequential change-point procedure (repeatedly splitting and testing) are not addressed.

Novelty positioning is incomplete. Distance-binned performance analysis is common practice (e.g., KITTI range-based evaluation), and prior work on confidence calibration and probabilistic detection quality (PDQ) already addresses output stochasticity; the paper asserts PCD's uniqueness but does not empirically compare against the most relevant baselines (e.g., simply reporting recall vs. distance curves, or distance-binned AP), which would be the natural alternative to aPCD and appears untested.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: standard frame-level metrics (AP, IoU, F1) do not capture distance-dependent degradation and stochastic fluctuation of detection confidence, which matters for threshold-based ADAS/ADS control logic. The motivating example in Figure 1 (fluctuating confidence at ≥70 m) is concrete and convincing.

PCD is a principled formulation: modeling IoU×confidence as a spline-estimated mean with segment-wise variance, using variance change point detection (SIC-based hypothesis testing from the statistics literature) to find where perception reliability degrades. The methodological details (Eq. 1–9) are specific and traceable to prior work [8, 15, 27].

The SensorRainFall dataset is a genuinely useful contribution: a controlled test-track collection (four weather/illumination conditions, camera/radar/LiDAR, DGPS-verified distances, manual box and mask annotations) that isolates environmental factors, which naturalistic datasets like BDD100K and nuScenes cannot do. Supplementary Table 2 gives useful descriptive statistics.

The benchmark is broad: 10 state-of-the-art detection/segmentation models across 16 experiment configurations, with complete results in the supplementary (Tables 3–10), including variance change point locations.
Section 5.3 provides simulation studies validating the change point detection component (sample size and effect size effects), rather than only asserting the statistical machinery works on real data.

The examples in Table 1 / Figures 5–6 are well chosen: they show cases where aPCD ranks models differently from AP/AR and explain the discrepancy qualitatively (lower variance, shorter failure tail), illustrating the complementary information the metric provides.
weaknesses: Scale and diversity of the dataset severely limit the generality of the claims. Only 1,231 images, a single ego-vehicle trajectory per condition, and exactly two target objects (one red sedan, one dummy pedestrian). Conclusions about 'perception system reliability' and a 'safety envelope' for ADS rest on very narrow data; the safety-envelope discussion in Section 5.2 (threshold recommendations for emergency braking, lane keeping, etc.) is largely speculative relative to the evidence.

The independence assumption underlying the likelihood-based change point test is questionable. Images are sequential frames from single runs, so IoU×confidence values at adjacent distances (and within segments) are temporally correlated and repeat passes over the same object; this inflates effective variance estimates and undermines the nominal α = 0.05 significance level. The paper does not discuss or address this.

Internal inconsistency in the data description: the main text states rainy conditions were conducted at 'a controlled rainfall rate of 64 mm/h' (Section 3), while the supplementary states two nominal intensities of 20 mm/h and 40 mm/h. This contradiction in a central experimental parameter raises concerns about the accuracy of the dataset documentation.

Validation of the metric's claimed superiority is mostly anecdotal. The paper reports that aPCD agrees with traditional metrics in 11 of 16 experiments and uses two cherry-picked disagreement examples to argue aPCD's value. There is no quantitative comparison against existing uncertainty-aware or temporal metrics (e.g., PDQ [13], stability metrics [39]), no downstream-task or safety-outcome validation, and no sensitivity analysis of how aPCD depends on the spline/change-point modeling choices.

The choice of IoU × confidence as the quality variable is ad hoc; alternatives (e.g., localized failure-rate vs. distance, calibration-aware scores) are not compared, and Section 4.2's justification is qualitative only.

Presentation and polish issues are numerous: incomplete URLs in the abstract (broken Kaggle/GitHub links), repeated sentences (e.g., 'The dataset includes both object-level...' appears twice on p.2), blank facility names ('Data were collected on the , a facility...'), an unfinished final sentence in the Conclusion ('while the broader societal impacts of full autonomy.'), a grammatically broken sentence in Section 5.3 ('illustrating ratio under 50–50 samples'), and a stray 'ok' in Table 9. These collectively suggest the manuscript was not carefully proofread.
Anonymization appears incomplete or mishandled: the test facility is left blank in the text yet reference [11] explicitly identifies Virginia's Smart Road, which likely de-anonymizes the submission.

Several experimental configurations appear saturated or degenerate (all-zero aPCD/AP for pedestrian instance segmentation in rainy night, Table 10), which is reported but not analyzed; models are also evaluated zero-shot without fine-tuning, and the paper does not discuss how this choice interacts with the conclusions.
